summary:
Our project is a health monitoring tool that helps astronauts understand their own health on long missions, without needing medical training.
Astronauts face five hazards that NASA names: radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, altered gravity and hostile closed environments. We built our app around those hazards. An astronaut logs simple readings, such as heart rate, blood pressure, sleep, mood and cabin air quality. Instead of relying only on fixed limits, the app compares each reading with the astronaut’s own baseline and trend, because the earliest warning sign is often a slow drift that still looks “normal” on paper. A clickable body figure shows green, yellow or red zones, and every indicator links to the space hazard behind it, with a plain-language explanation and one clear first step.
Because messages to Earth can take up to about 20 minutes each way on the way to Mars, the app escalates in stages: self-care, the crew medical officer, then the ground flight surgeon. It never makes the crew wait for a reply.
It matters because the farther humans travel, the more they must look after their own health. We use clearly labelled demonstration data, and the project is open source.
details:
What it does and how it works

Our project is a health monitoring tool that helps astronauts understand their own health on long missions, with no medical training needed. The astronaut logs simple readings such as heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, temperature, sleep, mood, breathing, exercise and cabin air quality. The app turns each one into a color: green, yellow, red, or flashing red for an emergency. A clickable body figure shows which part of the body needs attention. Tapping a zone shows a 14-day chart, a plain-language explanation of what the reading means, one clear first step, and who to tell.

Each reading is checked in two ways: against a published healthy range, and against the astronaut’s own baseline and trend. A slow drift, like a rising resting heart rate after several nights of poor sleep, can still look “normal” on paper. We built the app to catch that drift early.

Benefits and intended impact

On a trip to Mars, messages can take up to about 20 minutes each way, so the crew must act first. Our app escalates in stages: self-care, then the crew medical officer, then the ground flight surgeon. It never waits for a reply. We want astronauts to spot problems early and know what to do next. The same idea can also help people on Earth in remote or isolated places.

Tools and technologies

We built the interface with React and TypeScript using Vercel hosting. We used Google Sheets to compile our research and data sources, with 17 health indicators, ranges, escalation rules and demo baselines in one shared sheet and Google Slides for presentation. All the data in our demo is synthetic and clearly labelled as such. No special hardware is required. The project is open source.

Our data sheet: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1F9bJKYlGqwi9E4o0Tmm4KBATNbKb58kLsGBgQ7YHV7o/edit?usp=sharing

What makes it creative

  • Every indicator is tied to one of NASA’s five hazards, so the app explains why something changes in space.
  • It compares each reading with the astronaut’s own baseline instead of one fixed limit.
  • The escalation steps are designed around communication delay.
  • The sheet marks every value as verified or assumed, so there are no hidden guesses.

What our team considered

We built our indicators from NASA’s Human Research Program and NASA’s own standards for radiation and cabin carbon dioxide limits. We used trusted health sources for vital signs. We are honest that demonstration values are not clinical guidance, and the app says so. We wrote every explanation for people with no medical training. We kept mental health information private, so mood alerts go first to the crew medical officer. Our three-person team built the project in 48 hours, so we focused on the core demo story first.
dataRefs: NASA: Ongoing HRP Research in Space (articles)
